card.hook: Picture this: a bronze statue, a few surfboards, a surfer paddling out, and a big green ridge sitting behind the lot. At Duke Kahanamoku Beach the postcard really does build itself.
card.stand_here: Stand at Duke Kahanamoku Beach, on the sand in front of the Duke Kahanamoku statue, and face Diamond Head. The statue and its surfboards will be up front, the beach and surfers in the middle, and Diamond Head behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the statue, the beach and Diamond Head all fit. Try 0.5x to make the statue look bigger up close, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull Diamond Head closer. The beachfront is busy, so shoot a little wider than you think you need and let people be part of the scene.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue, then slide the picture a touch darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Sunset is the time guides recommend, though the light changes with the season and the beachfront gets crowded. Sunrise can be shaded by tall hotels in some areas.
card.selfie_here: Try the beach jetty just to the left of the pink Royal Hawaiian hotel. It gets early-morning light and sits a little farther from the tall hotels, so use the front camera (or 0.5x) and keep the beach behind you with fewer people in the shot. The beach and lagoon at the Hilton Hawaiian Village, near the Rainbow Tower, is another good option.
card.ask_someone: Walk out on the short concrete pier behind the Outrigger Reef (public access paths run on either side, near Fort DeRussy Park) and ask a passer-by to take your photo with the beach behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is an open public beach and park area, but check the official site before you go in case of events or closures. Waves can be stronger on windy days, and sea air and sun cream smear your phone's camera glass, so give it a wipe first.
card.challenge: Get the statue, a surfer and Diamond Head all in one frame, then see who in your group spots the outrigger canoe first.
card.good_to_know: Waikiki was briefly the first capital of the Kingdom of Hawaii (1795 to 1796) and later a retreat for Hawaiian royalty, who surfed here. Duke Kahanamoku, a famous surfer, helped make it a surfing hotspot. The sand is almost entirely man-made, shipped in from California in the 1920s and 1930s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Duke Kahanamoku Beach, on the sand in front of the Duke Kahanamoku statue, and face Diamond Head. The statue and its surfboards will be up front, the beach and surfers in the middle, and Diamond Head behind.

selfie_spots.why: The jetty gets early-morning light and lets you stand a little farther from the tall hotels, so the beach is behind you with fewer people in the shot.

selfie_research.notes: The pages I found mostly describe Diamond Head as the backdrop rather than Waikiki Beach itself, so the selfie spots above are the best fits, not exact matches. The ask-someone spot comes from a photography blog that describes the pier as good for shots with the beach behind; it does not give instructions for a passer-by, so the framing is my inference from that description. No page I found states rules on selfie sticks or tripods for these beaches, so none are reported.

card.hook: Here's the twist: the best view of Diamond Head isn't from the top. Up there you're looking out at Waikiki, so you never see the crater shape you came for.
card.stand_here: Head to the middle of Kapiolani Park, near the tennis courts, and face the crater. From there it rises right above the open lawns, with the crater centred in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the crater, the lawn and the sky all fit. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the ridge closer. Zoom 0.5x only works if you want lots of lawn, because the crater will look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the crater slope, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the slope doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the park is often empty. You'll get a cleaner shot with fewer strangers wandering through it.
card.selfie_here: Take it in Kapiʻolani Regional Park with the crater behind you, well away from the summit crowds. Use the front camera and hold it a bit low so the big slope fills the space over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Recreational drones aren't permitted, and take care near steep edges. If you hike the summit trail, visitors from outside Hawaii need an online reservation and the trail has set hours, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and sit the ridgeline along one horizontal line, with a strip of lawn at the bottom. Then see if you can spot the tuna's dorsal fin.
card.good_to_know: Hawaiians call it Lēʻahi, probably because the ridgeline looks like the dorsal fin of a tuna. British sailors renamed it in 1825 after mistaking sparkling calcite crystals in the sand for diamonds. It's a volcanic tuff cone roughly 400,000 to 500,000 years old, and it has been a National Natural Landmark since 1968.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the middle of Kapiolani Park, near the tennis courts, and face the crater. From there it rises right above the open lawns, with the crater centred in your frame.

selfie_spots.why: Bloggers call this the 'Instagram spot' where a selfie can have a clear view behind you, though it is hard to fit both the view and the bunker in one frame.

card.hook: The Moana Surfrider just sits there in its white Victorian glory while Kalakaua Avenue rushes by in front of it. That contrast is the whole fun of this shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement across Kalakaua Avenue from the hotel's entrance, near the ABC store. From the 2365 Kalakaua Avenue spot, the hotel is to the south-west, so face that way and stay on the public pavement.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the whole front fits in from across the avenue. Switch to 1x for a calmer view with less stretching at the edges. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the columns and the porch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's straight vertical edges with them, so those columns stand up tall.
card.best_time: Early evening, when the hotel is lit up, is a good bet, and night mode helps once it gets dark. Early morning should be calmer, with fewer people crossing in front of you.
card.selfie_here: Walk through from Kalakaua Avenue to the banyan courtyard and stand under the big tree, with the front camera held a little low so the branches and roots fill the space behind you. Or go to the sand at Waikiki Beach in front of the hotel, face away from the water, and use 0.5x so the beachfront wing fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Kalakaua Avenue sidewalk across from the hotel's porte cochère entrance, while you pose in front of the hotel so they can fit the columns and gallery behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The hotel is private property, so take photos from public areas and be considerate of guests. Cross Kalakaua Avenue at a proper crossing, not between the traffic. Check the hotel's official site before you go for courtyard access and any renovation closures.
card.challenge: Hold your shot until the people crossing the street leave a clean gap, then snap it and see if you can make the columns look perfectly straight.
card.good_to_know: The oldest part of the Moana Surfrider opened in 1901 as the first hotel in Waikiki, and it's listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Two floors and the side wings were added in 1918, which gave it the H-shape you see today. The banyan in the courtyard was planted in 1904 and is now about 23 m (75 ft) high and 46 m (150 ft) across.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the pavement across Kalakaua Avenue from the hotel's entrance, near the ABC store. From the 2365 Kalakaua Avenue spot, the hotel is to the south-west, so face that way and stay on the public pavement.

selfie_spots.why: A visitor photo from the beach looks back at the hotel, so the historic building fills the frame behind the person.

card.hook: Most statehouses look like a wedding cake. This one looks like an island: palm-tree columns, volcano-shaped chambers and the sky for a dome. Your photo practically composes itself.
card.stand_here: Head to the Beretania Street front entrance, near the Father Damien statue. Face the building so the statue sits in front and the columns rise behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the facade and statue together. If you're close and the columns won't fit, tap 0.5x. Save 2x for details like the statue or the tops of the columns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the statue low in the frame and hold your phone level so the columns don't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the bright part of the day, when the facade is evenly lit. Check current conditions around the building first, since plywood has surrounded it since 2020.
card.selfie_here: Try the Liberty Bell on the Beretania Street side. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x, and step back so the building fits over your shoulder. Check the preview, because we can't promise the full facade will line up behind you from here.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand by the Eternal Flame, directly across Beretania Street, while you stand in front of the Capitol so they can fit the whole building in.
card.rules_and_safety: Access to the Capitol and its courtyard may be restricted during sessions or events, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Count the palm-shaped columns on one side, then see if you can fit all eight in one shot.
card.good_to_know: The Capitol opened on 15 March 1969 and replaced ʻIolani Palace as the seat of government. The eight columns in each row stand for the eight main islands. The reflecting pool has been empty since 2020, so don't expect water in your photos.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the Beretania Street front entrance, near the Father Damien statue. Face the building so the statue sits in front and the columns rise behind it.

card.hook: You won't need to hunt for this one. The Royal Hawaiian is a huge pink hotel on Waikiki's seafront, and it looks a bit like a birthday cake that grew up.
card.stand_here: Head for The Royal Hawaiian on Kalakaua Avenue. The hotel's centre is to the south, about 2 minutes on foot. Stand at the Kalakaua Avenue entrance by the porte cochère (the covered drive-up entrance) and face the pink front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the pink front and the arched entrance. Tap 0.5x if the building won't fit, or if you want the palms and the drive in the shot. Try 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the cupolas and the arch details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with them so the pink walls stay nice and straight.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when it's quietest and fewer people wander through your shot. The beach side looks best in early morning light too.
card.selfie_here: Try the Coconut Grove courtyard in the hotel's garden. Stand with the historic wing and the Royal Hawaiian sign behind you, use the front camera, and tap 0.5x if your phone has it so more of the scene squeezes in. The Ocean Lawn also works: stand between the 1927 wing and Waikiki Beach with the pink facade over your shoulder. A wedding photographer says golden hour light is strongest there.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the sand of Royal Hawaiian Beach facing the hotel, while you stand between them and the pink front, and ask them to step back if the whole building won't fit.
card.rules_and_safety: The Royal Hawaiian is a working hotel, so check the official site to see which parts of the entrance and grounds you can use. The Ocean Lawn is also used for events, so check for a wedding or function before you go.
card.challenge: Get the arch right in the middle, with a palm on each side and not a single stranger's head in the frame.
card.good_to_know: The Royal Hawaiian opened on 1 February 1927 with a black-tie gala. The New York firm Warren and Wetmore designed it in a Spanish and Moorish style, and the cupolas were made to look like Spanish Mission bell towers. It has six storeys, 400 rooms and a garden of about 15 acres, and it goes by the nickname "The Pink Palace of the Pacific".
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for The Royal Hawaiian on Kalakaua Avenue. The hotel's centre is to the south, about 2 minutes on foot. Stand at the Kalakaua Avenue entrance by the porte cochère (the covered drive-up entrance) and face the pink front.

card.hook: Picture a long straight path running right up to a royal palace, like the whole place was built for your photo. ʻIolani Palace was home to Hawaiʻi's rulers, and it's the only royal palace on US soil.
card.stand_here: Stand on the front walkway of ʻIolani Palace, right on the phone icon, and face the main façade. The icon sits at the palace itself, so you can't really miss it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole palace in. If you're too close to step back, try 0.5x. Use 2x or more to pick out details of the building.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the walkway up with the middle of the building, then tap the palace and drag the slider a touch darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the stone.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon. Side light warms the stone and the koa-wood details, so the palace looks its best.
card.selfie_here: Head to the verandas of ʻIolani Palace and stand between the arches and columns with the building behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the layered columns frame you. Soft morning or late afternoon light is flattering here.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the front lawn, use the walkway as a leading line, and step back so you on the walkway, the full façade, the palms and the sky all fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: No flash, and selfie sticks aren't allowed, so keep your phone in your hand. Please don't pose on the Coronation Pavilion or the palace steps, as they're not available for private use. The grounds gates may be locked outside visiting hours, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the walkway pointing straight at the doors, then one with palms and sky above. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: ʻIolani Palace was the royal residence of Hawaiʻi's rulers from Kamehameha III in 1845 to Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893. After the monarchy ended, it was the seat of government until 1969. It was then restored and opened as a museum in 1978.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the front walkway of ʻIolani Palace, right on the phone icon, and face the main façade. The icon sits at the palace itself, so you can't really miss it.

selfie_spots.why: The verandas give layered columns and arches as a backdrop, and a guide notes soft side light makes a portrait there work well, especially in the morning or late afternoon.

card.hook: Magic Island isn't a natural island at all, but the view from its tip is so good nobody seems to mind. Ocean, skyline, mountains and Diamond Head all squeeze into one frame.
card.stand_here: Come in from the Kaka'ako footbridge: the middle of the park is 139 m away, about 2 minutes on foot to the north-west. Then keep going out along Magic Island to the tip of the lagoon and face the water, so the ocean, the Honolulu skyline, the Ko'olau mountains and Diamond Head sit in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to take in the lagoon, sky and shoreline together. Switch to 1x for a more natural look at the skyline and mountains, then try 2x or 5x (if your phone has them) to pull Diamond Head and the city closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky, then slide the brightness darker a little so the sunset colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Around sunset is the usual pick. Weekends, holidays and Friday fireworks nights get very busy, so arrive early to claim a clear spot.
card.selfie_here: Try the Sunset Lookout on the Magic Island peninsula, with the park's shoreline and lagoon behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so you and the view both fit, and tilt the phone up a touch to keep the sky in.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is closed overnight from 10:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m., so check the official site for closures or parking changes. There are lifeguard towers at Ala Moana, according to a visitor guide.
card.challenge: Can you get all four in one frame: open ocean, skyline, mountains and Diamond Head? Bonus points if the horizon sits neatly on a gridline.
card.good_to_know: The whole park sits on made land. It was marshland until it was filled in with dredged material in the 1930s. Magic Island came along in 1962, built from about thirty acres of reclaimed reef, and was meant to be the first of several islands until public objection stopped the plan. The state later gave it the Hawaiian name 'Aina Moana, though locals still say Magic Island.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Come in from the Kaka'ako footbridge: the middle of the park is 139 m away, about 2 minutes on foot to the north-west. Then keep going out along Magic Island to the tip of the lagoon and face the water, so the ocean, the Honolulu skyline, the Ko'olau mountains and Diamond Head sit in front of you.

card.hook: Most places make you choose between the beach and the fish. Here you get both, because the aquarium sits right on the Waikīkī shoreline, built beside a living coral reef.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon, in the middle of the Waikīkī Aquarium site. Face the building with the water beside it, so both fit in one picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the building and the shoreline together. Switch to 1x for most shots, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for sculpture or coral details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the fish or coral, then slide the picture a touch darker so bright water doesn't wash out the colours.
card.best_time: Outside, morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the shoreline. Inside, any time works because the tanks are lit, but check the official site for visiting times first.
card.selfie_here: Try the park side of Kalakaua Avenue, across from the aquarium entrance, so the building is behind you. Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder. This one is our best guess from the layout, so see what works on the day.
card.rules_and_safety: One guide says photos are fine without flash, so keep it off. Keep an eye on children around open tanks. Check the official site for entry details and what you can photograph.
card.challenge: Collect a set of three: the building with the sea, one fish all to itself, and a close-up of coral or the Jun Kaneko sculptures.
card.good_to_know: The aquarium opened in 1904 and is the second-oldest public aquarium still running in the United States. It moved to its present site in 1955. Today it looks after more than 3,500 marine plants and animals of about 490 species, and one giant clam here was 38 years old in 2016.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon, in the middle of the Waikīkī Aquarium site. Face the building with the water beside it, so both fit in one picture.

One Honolulu Magazine page says a photographer takes group photos inside the aquarium, not outside, so it doesn't count as a passer-by spot. card.hook: Red columns, a green roof and fishtail palms, and you haven't even stepped into the garden yet. It's a very colourful way to start.
card.stand_here: Stand at Kuan Yin Temple, by the garden entrance on the temple side, outside the garden's grounds. From the corner of Nu'uanu Avenue and North Vineyard Boulevard it's about 1 minute on foot to the north-west. Face the temple so the green roof and red columns fill the picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the temple and entrance. If you're squeezed for space, switch to 0.5x to fit the whole roof and columns in. Inside, try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the Buddha replica or for palm and orchid details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the temple, then slide the brightness down a touch so the red and green don't wash out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light and richer colour than midday. Check the garden's current opening hours before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the gazebo on Bo Terrace inside the garden, where you can pose with the white gazebo behind you. Or head to the lower lawn beside the driftwood arches, which act like natural frames. Use the front camera and hold it low so the canopy fills the shot, or switch to 0.5x to fit more in.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is fine, but wedding or commercial shoots need a city permit, and drones aren't allowed without one. Some paths have gentle slopes, so watch your footing. The garden may have admission, opening hours and photography rules, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, line up the red columns with the vertical lines, and tuck one palm leaf into the corner for a tropical frame.
card.good_to_know: Foster is the oldest botanical garden in Hawaii, and it's on the National Register of Historic Places. It began in 1853, when German doctor and botanist William Hillebrand leased the land and planted trees, and many of the big trees on the Upper Terrace are his. Mary Foster left the property to the city in 1930 so it would stay a public tropical park. Look out for the Sacred Fig, a clone descendant of the Bodhi tree Buddha sat under.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Kuan Yin Temple, by the garden entrance on the temple side, outside the garden's grounds. From the corner of Nu'uanu Avenue and North Vineyard Boulevard it's about 1 minute on foot to the north-west. Face the temple so the green roof and red columns fill the picture.

card.hook: Picture your friend in a fresh lei, grinning under an arch, with a lane of market stalls running off behind them. That's the best single frame in Honolulu's Chinatown, and it's easier to get than it sounds.
card.stand_here: Walk north from the spot on the map into the district to the Chinatown Gateway arch, then stand under the arch. Face the lane of lei and market stalls beyond it, and have your friend stand just inside the arch while you step back a little.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the arch frames your friend with the stalls behind. Try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the lei, and save zoom 0.5x for the long street views, keeping people away from the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the arch up with the vertical lines so it looks nice and straight.
card.best_time: Shop opening times vary, so check before you go. Most buildings here are four storeys or less, so light reaches the street.
card.selfie_here: Take it under the Chinatown Gateway arch after picking up a lei on Maunakea Street. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the arch over your shoulder. For a second one, try the sidewalk at the corner of Maunakea and Hotel streets, in front of the pink, pagoda-roofed Wo Fat building.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask first if you photograph people at work, and keep a friendly distance. Use ordinary city awareness here, especially after dark.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the lei is the star and the stalls behind are just a soft, colourful blur. Bonus points if your friend's smile survives the third retake.
card.good_to_know: Labourers brought from China to work on Hawaii's sugar plantations often became merchants here once their contracts ended. Fires in 1886 and 1900 destroyed most of the neighbourhood, and many buildings you see today date from 1901 onwards. The Oahu Market, opened in 1904, is still used for fresh fish and produce.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk north from the spot on the map into the district to the Chinatown Gateway arch, then stand under the arch. Face the lane of lei and market stalls beyond it, and have your friend stand just inside the arch while you step back a little.

card.hook: A gold-cloaked king stands against a pale government building, with palm trees lining the street behind him. It's one of the easiest "wow, that looks good" shots in downtown Honolulu.
card.stand_here: Stand on South King Street, across King Street from the statue on the Iolani Palace side. The statue is about 1 minute on foot away, to the south-west, so face south-west and you'll have Aliʻiōlani Hale right behind him.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole statue with the building behind. Go to 0.5x for more of the building and the palm-lined street. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the face, the gilded cloak and the plinth panels.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the gold cloak, and if the sky looks washed out, nudge the picture a little darker.
card.best_time: Go in daylight. Early morning and late afternoon give softer light and fewer crowds. On 11 June, Kamehameha Day, the statue is draped in long lei, which makes a special photo, but the crowds are heavy.
card.selfie_here: Step into the courtyard right in front of the statue, on the King Street side. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low so the king is right over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sidewalk across South King Street, facing the statue and Aliʻiōlani Hale, while you stand in front of the statue.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't climb or sit on the statue base. King Street is one-way with a lot of traffic and tour buses, so keep well back from the kerb while you frame your shot.
card.challenge: Can you fit the statue, the building behind it and a peek of Iolani Palace in one frame? Then zoom in and catch one of the four gilded panels on the plinth.
card.good_to_know: The statue was made by American sculptor Thomas Ridgeway Gould and erected in 1883. It's the second cast of the design. The first sank with its ship near the Falkland Islands, and the replacement was paid for with the insurance money. The first cast was recovered later and now stands in North Kohala on Hawaiʻi island.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on South King Street, across King Street from the statue on the Iolani Palace side. The statue is about 1 minute on foot away, to the south-west, so face south-west and you'll have Aliʻiōlani Hale right behind him.
